analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: Bovine Respiratory Disease (BRD) is a significant economic and clinical health challenge affecting calves,with limited knowledge about UK farm veterinarians' decision-making regarding antibiotic use in BRD 治疗.该研究旨在通过检查英国农场兽医对犊牛 BRD 抗生素处方的影响决策过程和背景因素来解决这一知识差距。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究采用了基于先前研究的调查设计,适合英国情况,并与农场兽医进行了试点。最终调查包含 28 个问题,包括多项选择题、文本输入题、李克特量表和数字排序问题,针对英国农场兽医。
analysis_zh.methods: 该调查是使用 Microsoft Word 设计的,并在 27 名农场兽医中进行了试点。反馈用于完善调查,其中包括有关临床症状、抗生素 治疗 选项和李克特量表重要性评估的问题。
analysis_zh.main_results: 调查发现,BRD 影响全球 12-16% 的断奶前奶牛犊,具有重大的经济和健康影响。该研究强调英国农场兽医需要更好地了解抗生素处方实践。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 该研究为英国农场兽医关于 BRD 使用抗生素的决策过程提供了新颖的见解,解决了该领域的重大知识空白。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果可以为抗菌药物管理政策和实践提供信息,有助于减少英国奶牛场生产系统中抗生素的使用和减轻抗菌药物耐药性。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究因其对调查数据的依赖而受到限制,这些数据可能无法完全体现抗生素决策的复杂性。由于调查的设计和样本量,证据强度中等。

title: Ratio of Postdischarge Emergency Department Visits to Readmissions by Diagnosis.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Pediatric readmissions and postdischarge emergency department (ED) visits are common measures of postdischarge use and vary across pediatric conditions. Although often studied separately, these outcomes represent a continuum of hospital reuse. We introduce the ED/READ ratio (the ratio of postdischarge ED visits to readmissions) to characterize diagnosis-specific patterns of hospital reuse across common pediatric conditions. METHODS: In this single-center retrospective cohort study, we included children aged 0 to 17 years discharged from an urban tertiary children's hospital between July 2016 and December 2019. We included primary All-Patient Refined Diagnosis-Related Groups comprising 1% or more of admissions. The primary outcome was the 30-day ED/READ ratio, calculated as the number of all-cause postdischarge ED visits divided by the number of all-cause readmissions within 30 days of discharge, computed for each diagnosis with 95% CIs. RESULTS: Among 16 518 hospitalizations from 11 728 patients, the overall 30-day postdischarge ED visit rate was 8.1% and the readmission rate was 9.2%. The 30-day ED/READ ratio ranged from 0.08 (95% CI, 0.05-0.12) for chemotherapy to 2.41 (95% CI, 1.50-3.33) for tonsil and adenoid procedures. Diagnoses with ratios significantly more than 1 included asthma, bronchiolitis and respiratory syncytial virus pneumonia, and gastroenteritis; ratios less than 1 included chemotherapy, sickle cell anemia crisis, and seizures. CONCLUSION: The ED/READ ratio is a descriptive metric that complements traditional measures by characterizing diagnosis-specific patterns of postdischarge reuse across care settings. Used alongside existing metrics, the ratio may help generate hypotheses about diagnosis-specific targets for improvement. Further research is needed to evaluate its reproducibility and applications across diverse settings.

analysis.summary_en: This single-center retrospective cohort study introduced the ED/READ ratio to characterize diagnosis-specific patterns of postdischarge hospital reuse among pediatric patients aged 0 to 17 years. Among 16,518 hospitalizations, the overall 30-day postdischarge ED visit rate was 8.1% and the readmission rate was 9.2%. The ED/READ ratio varied widely by diagnosis, ranging from 0.08 for chemotherapy to 2.41 for tonsil and adenoid procedures. Diagnoses such as asthma, bronchiolitis, and gastroenteritis had ratios significantly greater than 1, indicating more frequent ED visits relative to readmissions, while chemotherapy, sickle cell anemia crisis, and seizures had ratios less than 1. title_zh: 诊断 出院后急诊科就诊与再入院的比率。
source_body_en: BACKGROUND: Pediatric readmissions and postdischarge emergency department (ED) visits are common measures of postdischarge use and vary across pediatric conditions. Although often studied separately, these outcomes represent a continuum of hospital reuse. We introduce the ED/READ ratio (the ratio of postdischarge ED visits to readmissions) to characterize diagnosis-specific patterns of hospital reuse across common pediatric conditions. METHODS: In this single-center retrospective cohort study, we included children aged 0 to 17 years discharged from an urban tertiary children's hospital between July 2016 and December 2019. We included primary All-Patient Refined Diagnosis-Related Groups comprising 1% or more of admissions. The primary outcome was the 30-day ED/READ ratio, calculated as the number of all-cause postdischarge ED visits divided by the number of all-cause readmissions within 30 days of discharge, computed for each diagnosis with 95% CIs. RESULTS: Among 16 518 hospitalizations from 11 728 patients, the overall 30-day postdischarge ED visit rate was 8.1% and the readmission rate was 9.2%. The 30-day ED/READ ratio ranged from 0.08 (95% CI, 0.05-0.12) for chemotherapy to 2.41 (95% CI, 1.50-3.33) for tonsil and adenoid procedures. Diagnoses with ratios significantly more than 1 included asthma, bronchiolitis and respiratory syncytial virus pneumonia, and gastroenteritis; ratios less than 1 included chemotherapy, sickle cell anemia crisis, and seizures. CONCLUSION: The ED/READ ratio is a descriptive metric that complements traditional measures by characterizing diagnosis-specific patterns of postdischarge reuse across care settings. Used alongside existing metrics, the ratio may help generate hypotheses about diagnosis-specific targets for improvement. Further research is needed to evaluate its reproducibility and applications across diverse settings.

title: Quality Improvement Initiative to Reduce Inappropriate Viral Testing within the Pediatric Emergency Department.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: The American Academy of Pediatrics Section on Emergency Medicine's Choosing Wisely Campaign includes recommendations discouraging comprehensive viral panel testing in children with suspected respiratory viral illness. In the year preceding project implementation, our free-standing pediatric emergency department (PED) ordered comprehensive respiratory pathogen panels (RPPs) in 11.9% of all visits, and 50% of those lacked a clinical indication. This project aimed to reduce the percentage of PED visits with RPP orders from 11.9% to 9% over a 6-month viral respiratory season. METHODS: We conducted four major interventions over 2 plan-do-study-act cycles. Interventions included developing a clinical guideline for viral testing, performing provider education, introducing a narrower-spectrum Quad (influenza A/B, COVID-19, and respiratory syncytial virus) polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test, and adding an order-entry indication requirement for RPPs, which also served as a just-in-time educational tool for providers. We tracked data via a clinical dashboard and through periodic chart reviews. RESULTS: Of the 43,283 patient visits during the project period, the percentage of PED RPP orders decreased from 11.9% at baseline to 6.8% during the intervention period and remained at 6.8% in the following respiratory season. The project had sustained cost savings of over $300,000 in RPP testing each year. The decrease in RPP orders did not lead to an increase in the cumulative use of other viral tests. CONCLUSIONS: This quality improvement initiative significantly improved and sustained comprehensive viral PCR testing practices in the PED without increasing the use of alternative respiratory viral testing.

analysis.scope_and_question: The review examines inappropriate viral testing practices in pediatric emergency departments (PEDs), focusing on comprehensive respiratory pathogen panels (RPPs) in children with suspected respiratory viral illness. The central question addresses reducing RPP orders from 11.9% to 9% over a 6-month viral respiratory season while maintaining appropriate diagnostic practices.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review describes a quality improvement initiative with four major interventions implemented over two plan-do-study-act cycles. Interventions included clinical guideline development, provider education, introduction of a narrower-spectrum Quad PCR test, and an order-entry indication requirement for RPPs. Data were tracked via a clinical dashboard and periodic chart reviews.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The initiative achieved a sustained reduction in RPP orders from 11.9% at baseline to 6.8% during the intervention period and maintained this reduction in the following respiratory season. The decrease did not result in increased use of alternative viral tests, and the project generated sustained cost savings exceeding $300,000 annually in RPP testing.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review does not report long-term clinical outcomes such as patient recovery rates, antibiotic use, or hospitalization rates following reduced RPP testing. Additionally, it does not address potential unintended consequences of reduced testing, such as missed diagnoses of less common viral pathogens.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review highlights the need for further research to evaluate the impact of reduced RPP testing on clinical outcomes, including patient safety and diagnostic accuracy for rare viral pathogens. It also suggests exploring the scalability of this quality improvement initiative to other healthcare settings and populations.

The initiative successfully reduced RPP orders to 6.8%, sustained over the following respiratory season, without increasing alternative viral testing. Annual cost savings exceeded $300,000. However, the review does not address long-term clinical outcomes or potential unintended consequences of reduced testing. Future research should assess patient safety and diagnostic accuracy impacts, while exploring scalability to other settings.

analysis_zh.scope_and_question: 该审查审查了儿科急诊科 (PED) 中不当的病毒检测做法,重点关注疑似呼吸道病毒性疾病儿童的综合呼吸道病原体检测 (RPP)。核心问题是在 6 个月的病毒呼吸道季节将 RPP 指令从 11.9% 减少到 9%,同时保持适当的诊断实践。
analysis_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 该审查描述了一项质量改进举措,其中包括在两个计划-实施-研究-行动周期中实施的四项主要干预措施。干预措施包括制定临床指南、提供者教育、引入窄谱四重 PCR 测试以及 RPP 的订单输入指示要求。通过临床仪表板和定期图表审查来跟踪数据。

title: Impacts of conventional and high-oleic soybean oil supplementation on rumen microbiology, physiology, immunity, and growth of recently weaned Brangus steers
abstract: Lay Summary High-oleic soybean oil (HOSBO) has a different fatty acid (FA) profile than conventional soybean oil (CSBO), which may lead to distinct effects on rumen microbiology, immune function, and growth when included in the diet of steers. Thus, the current experiment evaluated the effects of HOSBO, CSBO, and no oil supplementation on rumen microbiology, physiology, immunity, and growth of Brangus steers maintained in a forage-based system during the preconditioning phase. Although HOSBO and CSBO supplementation had minimal effects on rumen microbiology, it altered circulating FA profiles. The CSBO increased serum linoleic acid, whereas the HOSBO increased oleic acid. These differences in circulating FA were associated with distinct vaccine responses: steers receiving CSBO had stronger antibody responses to bovine viral diarrhea virus (BVDV), whereas those receiving HOSBO mounted stronger responses to bovine respiratory syncytial virus (BRSV). Growth also differed, with HOSBO-supplemented steers tending to be heavier than steers receiving CSBO by the end of the experiment. Overall, CSBO or HOSBO had minimal effects on rumen microbiology, but CSBO enhanced the immune response to BVDV, HOSBO enhanced the response to BRSV, and HOSBO promoted greater growth than CSBO.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addressed whether high-oleic soybean oil (HOSBO) and conventional soybean oil (CSBO) differentially affect rumen microbiology, immune function, and growth in recently weaned Brangus steers, given their distinct fatty acid profiles.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The experiment compared HOSBO, CSBO, and no oil supplementation in Brangus steers during a forage-based preconditioning phase to evaluate rumen microbiology, physiology, immunity, and growth.
analysis.methods: The study assessed rumen microbiology and measured circulating fatty acid profiles, vaccine responses to bovine viral diarrhea virus (BVDV) and bovine respiratory syncytial virus (BRSV), and growth outcomes in steers receiving different oil supplements.
analysis.main_results: CSBO increased serum linoleic acid, while HOSBO increased oleic acid, with CSBO enhancing antibody responses to BVDV and HOSBO enhancing responses to BRSV, and HOSBO-supplemented steers tending to be heavier than CSBO-supplemented steers by the end of the experiment.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that distinct fatty acid profiles in HOSBO and CSBO differentially modulate immune responses and growth in steers, highlighting potential dietary strategies to influence vaccine efficacy and performance.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results imply that soybean oil supplementation type may be tailored to optimize immune responses to specific viral pathogens and improve growth outcomes in cattle, informing nutritional management practices.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is limited to a single experiment in Brangus steers under forage-based conditions, with minimal effects on rumen microbiology and no reported statistical significance for growth differences, warranting cautious interpretation.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the effects of high-oleic soybean oil (HOSBO) and conventional soybean oil (CSBO) on rumen microbiology, immune function, and growth in recently weaned Brangus steers. While both oils minimally impacted rumen microbiology, they altered circulating fatty acid profiles: CSBO increased serum linoleic acid and enhanced antibody responses to bovine viral diarrhea virus (BVDV), whereas HOSBO increased oleic acid and improved responses to bovine respiratory syncytial virus (BRSV). Growth outcomes favored HOSBO, with supplemented steers tending to be heavier than CSBO-supplemented counterparts by the study's end. The findings suggest dietary oil type may modulate immune responses and growth in cattle, offering potential strategies for optimizing vaccine efficacy and performance through nutritional interventions.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究探讨了高油酸大豆油 (HOSBO) 和传统大豆油 (CSBO) 是否对最近断奶的布兰格斯公牛的瘤胃微生物、免疫功能和生长产生不同的影响,因为它们具有不同的脂肪酸谱。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该实验比较了 Brangus 公牛在基于饲料的预处理阶段中的 HOSBO、CSBO 和不补充油的情况,以评估瘤胃微生物学、生理学、免疫和生长。
elements_zh.methods: 该研究评估了瘤胃微生物学并测量了循环脂肪酸谱、疫苗 对牛病毒性腹泻病毒 (BVDV) 和牛 呼吸道合胞病毒 (BRSV) 的反应,以及接受不同油补充剂的公牛的生长结果。
elements_zh.main_results: CSBO 增加了血清亚油酸,而 HOSBO 增加了油酸,CSBO 增强了对 BVDV 的抗体反应,HOSBO 增强了对 BRSV 的反应,并且在实验结束时补充 HOSBO 的阉牛往往比补充 CSBO 的阉牛更重。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果表明,HOSBO 和 CSBO 中不同的脂肪酸谱对 免疫应答 和阉牛的生长有差异性调节,强调了影响 疫苗 功效和性能的潜在饮食策略。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 结果表明,大豆油补充剂类型可以根据特定病毒病原体优化 免疫应答,并改善牛的生长结果,为营养管理实践提供信息。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 证据仅限于在以饲料为基础的条件下对白朗格斯阉牛进行的一次实验,对瘤胃微生物学的影响很小,并且没有报道生长差异的统计显着性,需要谨慎解释。

title: Epidemiology, Clinical Characteristics, and Severity of Human Parainfluenza Virus Infection in Children from 2015-2025: A Scoping Review Protocol
abstract: The objective of this scoping review is to identify and map the available evidence on the epidemiology, clinical characteristics, and severity of HPIV infection in hospitalised children, and to identify comparisons within HPIV serotypes, with other respiratory viruses and risk factors for severe outcomes. Expected outcomes: - Evidence on the epidemiology, clinical characteristics, and severity of human parainfluenza virus (HPIV) infection in hospitalised children from 2015-2025 - The differences between HPIV serotypes (HPIV 1-4) in terms of epidemiology and clinical presentation - Comparison with other common respiratory viruses (e.g., RSV, influenza, human metapneumovirus) in terms of epidemiology and clinical severity - Risk factors associated with severe outcomes/re-admission of HPIV infection in children

source_records.title: Epidemiology, Clinical Characteristics, and Severity of Human Parainfluenza Virus Infection in Children from 2015-2025: A Scoping Review Protocol
source_records.abstract: The objective of this scoping review is to identify and map the available evidence on the epidemiology, clinical characteristics, and severity of HPIV infection in hospitalised children, and to identify comparisons within HPIV serotypes, with other respiratory viruses and risk factors for severe outcomes. Expected outcomes: - Evidence on the epidemiology, clinical characteristics, and severity of human parainfluenza virus (HPIV) infection in hospitalised children from 2015-2025 - The differences between HPIV serotypes (HPIV 1-4) in terms of epidemiology and clinical presentation - Comparison with other common respiratory viruses (e.g., RSV, influenza, human metapneumovirus) in terms of epidemiology and clinical severity - Risk factors associated with severe outcomes/re-admission of HPIV infection in children

title: Dynamic regulation-based stabilizing mutations are highly effective for designing RSV pre-fusion F mRNA vaccines
abstract: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a leading cause of respiratory tract infections and poses a serious threat to young children, older adults, and immunocompromised individuals. We previously designed a pre-fusion stabilized F protein (pre-F), TriM-5, using a dynamic regulation mechanism, and produced a recombinant protein-based vaccine candidate that exhibited potent protection against RSV. However, several studies have revealed that the stabilization of pre-F achieved in protein form may not be sufficient for application in mRNA vaccine development. Here, based on TriM-5, we designed an mRNA vaccine candidate to assess whether the dynamic regulation-based stabilizing mutations of TriM-5 are also effective in an mRNA format. The TriM-5 mRNA was codon-optimized using in-house software named NVSI_GAmRNAopt, which employed a genetic algorithm incorporating multiple empirical parameters for coding sequence (CDS) optimization, and encapsulated using lipid nanoparticles (LNPs). Mouse immunization showed that after CDS optimization, the IgG antibody titers increased approximately threefold, indicating the effectiveness of our codon-optimization algorithm. Compared with the Moderna RSV mRNA sequence encapsulated with our proprietary BM028 LNPs, the TriM-5 mRNA-LNP induced 3.03-fold higher neutralizing antibody titers against RSV A2 virus, along with significantly higher IFN-γ, IL-5 and IL-17A secretion levels, indicating its superior immunogenicity. Virus challenge experiments demonstrated that both TriM-5 mRNA-LNP and Moderna mRNA-LNP reduced lung viral loads effectively, with no obvious lung pathology. The designed TriM-5 mRNA-LNP exhibits good immunogenicity and protective efficacy, and thereby may serve as a promising candidate for further vaccine development.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a major cause of severe respiratory infections in vulnerable populations, and current vaccine strategies face challenges in maintaining pre-fusion F protein stability, particularly in mRNA formats. The study aimed to determine whether dynamic regulation-based stabilizing mutations effective in protein-based RSV vaccines could translate to an mRNA vaccine candidate.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study evaluated a pre-fusion stabilized F protein (TriM-5) mRNA vaccine candidate in mice, comparing it to a Moderna RSV mRNA vaccine encapsulated in proprietary lipid nanoparticles (LNPs). The TriM-5 mRNA was codon-optimized using an in-house algorithm and encapsulated in LNPs for delivery.
analysis.methods: The TriM-5 mRNA sequence was codon-optimized using the NVSI_GAmRNAopt software, which employs a genetic algorithm with empirical parameters for coding sequence optimization, and encapsulated in lipid nanoparticles (LNPs). Mouse immunization assessed immunogenicity, including IgG antibody titers, neutralizing antibody titers, cytokine secretion (IFN-γ, IL-5, IL-17A), and protective efficacy via viral challenge.
analysis.main_results: Mouse immunization showed that codon-optimized TriM-5 mRNA-LNP induced approximately threefold higher IgG antibody titers compared to unoptimized sequences. The TriM-5 mRNA-LNP induced 3.03-fold higher neutralizing antibody titers against RSV A2 virus than the Moderna RSV mRNA-LNP, along with significantly higher levels of IFN-γ, IL-5, and IL-17A. Both vaccines reduced lung viral loads effectively in challenge experiments, with no obvious lung pathology observed.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings demonstrate that dynamic regulation-based stabilizing mutations effective in protein-based RSV vaccines also enhance immunogenicity in an mRNA format, representing a novel approach to mRNA vaccine design for RSV. The superior immunogenicity of TriM-5 mRNA-LNP compared to a Moderna RSV mRNA vaccine highlights the potential of codon optimization and stabilization strategies in mRNA vaccine development.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results suggest that TriM-5 mRNA-LNP could serve as a promising candidate for further RSV vaccine development, potentially improving immunogenicity and protective efficacy in vulnerable populations. The study provides evidence that stabilization strategies effective in protein-based vaccines may be successfully adapted to mRNA platforms.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is limited to preclinical mouse studies, and the findings may not fully translate to human responses. While the study demonstrates superior immunogenicity and protective efficacy in mice, further research is needed to validate these results in clinical settings and assess long-term safety and efficacy.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated whether dynamic regulation-based stabilizing mutations effective in a protein-based RSV vaccine (TriM-5) could enhance immunogenicity in an mRNA format. The authors designed a codon-optimized TriM-5 mRNA vaccine encapsulated in lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) and evaluated its immunogenicity and protective efficacy in mice compared to a Moderna RSV mRNA vaccine. The TriM-5 mRNA-LNP induced significantly higher IgG and neutralizing antibody titers, as well as elevated cytokine responses (IFN-γ, IL-5, IL-17A), and reduced lung viral loads without pathology in challenge experiments. These findings suggest that stabilization strategies from protein-based vaccines can be successfully adapted to mRNA platforms, offering a promising candidate for further RSV vaccine development. However, the study is limited to preclinical mouse models, and human validation is required.

analysis_en.research_question_and_background: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a major cause of severe respiratory infections in vulnerable populations, and current vaccine strategies face challenges in maintaining pre-fusion F protein stability, particularly in mRNA formats. The study aimed to determine whether dynamic regulation-based stabilizing mutations effective in protein-based RSV vaccines could translate to an mRNA vaccine candidate.
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: The study evaluated a pre-fusion stabilized F protein (TriM-5) mRNA vaccine candidate in mice, comparing it to a Moderna RSV mRNA vaccine encapsulated in proprietary lipid nanoparticles (LNPs). The TriM-5 mRNA was codon-optimized using an in-house algorithm and encapsulated in LNPs for delivery.
analysis_en.methods: The TriM-5 mRNA sequence was codon-optimized using the NVSI_GAmRNAopt software, which employs a genetic algorithm with empirical parameters for coding sequence optimization, and encapsulated in lipid nanoparticles (LNPs). Mouse immunization assessed immunogenicity, including IgG antibody titers, neutralizing antibody titers, cytokine secretion (IFN-γ, IL-5, IL-17A), and protective efficacy via viral challenge.
analysis_en.main_results: Mouse immunization showed that codon-optimized TriM-5 mRNA-LNP induced approximately threefold higher IgG antibody titers compared to unoptimized sequences. The TriM-5 mRNA-LNP induced 3.03-fold higher neutralizing antibody titers against RSV A2 virus than the Moderna RSV mRNA-LNP, along with significantly higher levels of IFN-γ, IL-5, and IL-17A. Both vaccines reduced lung viral loads effectively in challenge experiments, with no obvious lung pathology observed.
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings demonstrate that dynamic regulation-based stabilizing mutations effective in protein-based RSV vaccines also enhance immunogenicity in an mRNA format, representing a novel approach to mRNA vaccine design for RSV. The superior immunogenicity of TriM-5 mRNA-LNP compared to a Moderna RSV mRNA vaccine highlights the potential of codon optimization and stabilization strategies in mRNA vaccine development.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results suggest that TriM-5 mRNA-LNP could serve as a promising candidate for further RSV vaccine development, potentially improving immunogenicity and protective efficacy in vulnerable populations. The study provides evidence that stabilization strategies effective in protein-based vaccines may be successfully adapted to mRNA platforms.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is limited to preclinical mouse studies, and the findings may not fully translate to human responses. While the study demonstrates superior immunogenicity and protective efficacy in mice, further research is needed to validate these results in clinical settings and assess long-term safety and efficacy.

title_zh: 基于动态调节的稳定 突变 对于设计 RSV 融合前 F mRNA 疫苗 非常有效
source_body_en: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a leading cause of respiratory tract infections and poses a serious threat to young children, older adults, and immunocompromised individuals. We previously designed a pre-fusion stabilized F protein (pre-F), TriM-5, using a dynamic regulation mechanism, and produced a recombinant protein-based vaccine candidate that exhibited potent protection against RSV. However, several studies have revealed that the stabilization of pre-F achieved in protein form may not be sufficient for application in mRNA vaccine development. Here, based on TriM-5, we designed an mRNA vaccine candidate to assess whether the dynamic regulation-based stabilizing mutations of TriM-5 are also effective in an mRNA format. The TriM-5 mRNA was codon-optimized using in-house software named NVSI_GAmRNAopt, which employed a genetic algorithm incorporating multiple empirical parameters for coding sequence (CDS) optimization, and encapsulated using lipid nanoparticles (LNPs). Mouse immunization showed that after CDS optimization, the IgG antibody titers increased approximately threefold, indicating the effectiveness of our codon-optimization algorithm. Compared with the Moderna RSV mRNA sequence encapsulated with our proprietary BM028 LNPs, the TriM-5 mRNA-LNP induced 3.03-fold higher neutralizing antibody titers against RSV A2 virus, along with significantly higher IFN-γ, IL-5 and IL-17A secretion levels, indicating its superior immunogenicity. Virus challenge experiments demonstrated that both TriM-5 mRNA-LNP and Moderna mRNA-LNP reduced lung viral loads effectively, with no obvious lung pathology. The designed TriM-5 mRNA-LNP exhibits good immunogenicity and protective efficacy, and thereby may serve as a promising candidate for further vaccine development.

title: A hierarchical clock-mixture model for Bayesian phylogenetic dating
abstract: Conditioning the inference of a Bayesian phylogenetic time tree on a single molecular clock model treats clock choice as fixed, even when support among plausible clock families is uncertain. When that assumption is wrong, estimated timescales and their uncertainty can be distorted. Existing practice usually addresses this by fitting strict, uncorrelated lognormal relaxed (UCLN), and autocorrelated clocks separately and comparing their marginal likelihoods, but this requires multiple computationally expensive model selection analyses.Here we introduce a hierarchical clock-mixture framework, implemented as the open-source \texttt{RelaxClockAveraging} package for BEAST~2, that separates two questions that are often conflated in clock comparison: whether branch-specific rate variation is needed at all, and, if it is, whether that variation is better described as uncorrelated or autocorrelated. The method averages analytically between strict and relaxed clocks at the top level and then compares UCLN and autocorrelated models within the relaxed class on a shared branch-rate vector, returning posterior probabilities for all three clock families together with model-averaged summaries for parameters shared across them. In stratified simulations, the generating clock family was retained in the 95\% posterior model set in all replicates, while model-averaged estimates of the overall substitution rate, root age, and tree length remained accurate. On a DENV-4 benchmark, the mixture reproduced the higher-effort nested-sampling ranking of clock families while avoiding the extreme run-to-run variability of independent marginal-likelihood estimates. On empirical benchmarks, the method recovered strong support for the autocorrelated clock on the classical 31-taxon chloroplast \textit{rbcL} data set. On an RSV-A G-gene data set it concentrated virtually all posterior support on UCLN while preserving the established RSV-A timescale. On a 245-taxon structured-coalescent H3N2 dataset it assigned most posterior mass to the relaxed-clock class, with support within that class concentrated on the autocorrelated family, and the inferred timescale remained consistent with the published estimate. These results show that clock-model support and downstream timescale sensitivity are related but not identical. Single-clock dating analyses can still be adequate, but fixing a clock model should be justified by posterior support rather than treated as a default assumption.

analysis.main_results: In stratified simulations, the generating clock family was retained in the 95% posterior model set in all replicates, and model-averaged estimates of the overall substitution rate, root age, and tree length remained accurate. elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 证据仅限于模拟和特定的经验数据集,可能无法完全捕捉现实世界系统发育场景的多样性。对于评估的基准来说,证据的强度很高,但仍有待在更广泛的数据集和条件下进行验证。

analysis_en.research_question_and_background: Current Bayesian phylogenetic dating often assumes a single fixed molecular clock model, which can distort estimated timescales and their uncertainty when the true clock family is uncertain. The study addresses the conflation of two questions in clock-model selection: whether branch-specific rate variation is needed and, if so, whether it is better described as uncorrelated or autocorrelated.
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: The study introduces a hierarchical clock-mixture framework implemented as the open-source RelaxClockAveraging package for BEAST 2. The method is evaluated using stratified simulations and empirical benchmarks including a DENV-4 dataset, a 31-taxon chloroplast rbcL dataset, an RSV-A G-gene dataset, and a 245-taxon structured-coalescent H3N2 dataset.
analysis_en.methods: The hierarchical clock-mixture model analytically averages between strict and relaxed clocks at the top level and compares uncorrelated lognormal (UCLN) and autocorrelated relaxed clocks within the relaxed class using a shared branch-rate vector. Posterior probabilities for all three clock families are returned, along with model-averaged summaries for shared parameters.
analysis_en.main_results: In stratified simulations, the generating clock family was retained in the 95% posterior model set in all replicates, and model-averaged estimates of the overall substitution rate, root age, and tree length remained accurate. On the DENV-4 benchmark, the mixture reproduced higher-effort nested-sampling rankings of clock families while avoiding extreme run-to-run variability of independent marginal-likelihood estimates.
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The results demonstrate that clock-model support and downstream timescale sensitivity are related but not identical, indicating that single-clock dating analyses can be adequate only when posterior support justifies the chosen clock model. The novelty lies in separating the two questions of clock-model selection and providing a computationally efficient framework for model averaging.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The hierarchical clock-mixture framework enables more accurate and reliable Bayesian phylogenetic dating by reducing distortions in timescale estimates caused by incorrect clock-model assumptions. This method supports robust inference in evolutionary studies and pathogen phylodynamics where accurate dating is critical.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is limited to simulations and specific empirical datasets, which may not fully capture the diversity of real-world phylogenetic scenarios. The strength of the evidence is high for the evaluated benchmarks but remains to be validated across broader datasets and conditions.

title_zh: 用于贝叶斯系统发育测年的分层时钟混合模型
source_body_en: Conditioning the inference of a Bayesian phylogenetic time tree on a single molecular clock model treats clock choice as fixed, even when support among plausible clock families is uncertain. When that assumption is wrong, estimated timescales and their uncertainty can be distorted. Existing practice usually addresses this by fitting strict, uncorrelated lognormal relaxed (UCLN), and autocorrelated clocks separately and comparing their marginal likelihoods, but this requires multiple computationally expensive model selection analyses.Here we introduce a hierarchical clock-mixture framework, implemented as the open-source \texttt{RelaxClockAveraging} package for BEAST~2, that separates two questions that are often conflated in clock comparison: whether branch-specific rate variation is needed at all, and, if it is, whether that variation is better described as uncorrelated or autocorrelated. The method averages analytically between strict and relaxed clocks at the top level and then compares UCLN and autocorrelated models within the relaxed class on a shared branch-rate vector, returning posterior probabilities for all three clock families together with model-averaged summaries for parameters shared across them. In stratified simulations, the generating clock family was retained in the 95\% posterior model set in all replicates, while model-averaged estimates of the overall substitution rate, root age, and tree length remained accurate. On a DENV-4 benchmark, the mixture reproduced the higher-effort nested-sampling ranking of clock families while avoiding the extreme run-to-run variability of independent marginal-likelihood estimates. On empirical benchmarks, the method recovered strong support for the autocorrelated clock on the classical 31-taxon chloroplast \textit{rbcL} data set. On an RSV-A G-gene data set it concentrated virtually all posterior support on UCLN while preserving the established RSV-A timescale. On a 245-taxon structured-coalescent H3N2 dataset it assigned most posterior mass to the relaxed-clock class, with support within that class concentrated on the autocorrelated family, and the inferred timescale remained consistent with the published estimate. These results show that clock-model support and downstream timescale sensitivity are related but not identical. Single-clock dating analyses can still be adequate, but fixing a clock model should be justified by posterior support rather than treated as a default assumption.
abstract_zh: 在贝叶斯系统发育时间树的推断中,若以单一分子钟模型为条件,则将钟模型的选择视为固定,即使在不同钟模型家系间的支持度存在不确定性。当这一假设不成立时,估计的时间尺度及其不确定性可能会被扭曲。现有做法通常通过分别拟合严格钟模型、无相关对数正态松弛钟模型(UCLN)及自相关钟模型,并比较其边缘似然值来解决这一问题,但此过程需进行多次计算成本高昂的模型选择分析。本研究引入一种分层钟混合框架,以开源 \texttt{RelaxClockAveraging} 软件包(适用于 BEAST 2)实现,将钟模型比较中常被混淆的两个问题分离:是否需要分支特异性速率变异,以及若需要,此变异是否更适合用无相关或自相关模型描述。该方法在顶层解析性地平均严格钟与松弛钟,并在松弛类内比较 UCLN 与自相关模型(基于共享的分支速率 媒介),同时返回三种钟模型家系的后验概率及跨模型共享参数的模型平均摘要。在分层模拟中,生成钟模型家系在 95\% 后验模型集中被保留于所有重复实验中,而总体替代速率、根节点年龄及树长的模型平均估计值保持准确。在登革病毒 4 型(DENV-4)基准测试中,该混合方法在避免独立边缘似然估计极端运行间变异性的同时,复现了嵌套抽样对钟模型家系的高工作量排序结果。在经验基准测试中,该方法在经典 31 样本叶绿体 \textit{rbcL} 数据集上恢复了对自相关钟模型的强支持。在呼吸道合胞病毒 A 型(RSV-A)G 基因数据集上,该方法将几乎所有后验支持集中于 UCLN,同时保留了已确立的 RSV-A 时间尺度。在包含 245 样本的结构化 coalescent H3N2 数据集上,该方法将大部分后验质量分配至松弛钟类,并在该类内将支持集中于自相关家系,且推断的时间尺度与已发表估计值保持一致。这些结果表明,钟模型支持度与下游时间尺度敏感性相关但并不相同。单一钟模型定年分析仍可能足够,但固定钟模型应基于后验支持而非默认假设进行论证。

full_text: Abstract Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) impairs STAT3 activation in infected ciliated cells in infants, but not adults, causing apoptosis to facilitate virus spread. How age regulates the STAT3 response to RSV in human bronchial epithelial cells (BEpiCs) is unknown. Here, we identify an age-associated immune-poised physiological state in human bronchial basal stem cells (BSCs) and progeny BEpiCs, rendering robust RIG-I to guard against the inactivation of RIG-I-STAT3 signaling by RSV nonstructural protein 2. In contrast, infant BEpiCs are vulnerable to such inactivation by RSV due to lower RIG-I levels. We show that acute respiratory viral infection in specific pathogen-free mice, rather than physical age, triggers sustained epigenetic and transcriptomic remodeling in BEpiCs that resembles age-associated changes in human BEpiCs. In addition, cytokine pretreatment of human neonatal BSCs induces an adult-like immune-poised state that is maintained in progeny BEpiCs to defend against RSV. Therefore, respiratory infection and inflammation during a lifetime imparts the effect of age to BSCs, which fortifies RIG-I in progeny cells to mitigate RSV infection. analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) impairs STAT3 activation in infected ciliated cells in infants but not adults, yet the mechanism by which age regulates the STAT3 response to RSV in human bronchial epithelial cells (BEpiCs) remains unknown.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study investigated age-associated immune-poised states in human bronchial basal stem cells (BSCs) and their progeny BEpiCs, comparing infant and adult cells, and used specific pathogen-free mice to model acute respiratory viral infection.
analysis.methods: The authors examined RIG-I levels and RIG-I-STAT3 signaling in human BSCs and BEpiCs, assessed epigenetic and transcriptomic remodeling in mouse BEpiCs following viral infection, and evaluated cytokine pretreatment effects on neonatal BSCs to induce adult-like states.
analysis.main_results: RSV nonstructural protein 2 inactivates RIG-I-STAT3 signaling in infant BEpiCs due to lower RIG-I levels, whereas adult BEpiCs maintain robust RIG-I signaling and resist inactivation, and acute viral infection in mice triggers sustained epigenetic and transcriptomic changes in BEpiCs resembling human age-associated states.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings reveal that prior respiratory infections and inflammation epigenetically program basal stem cells to fortify RIG-I in progeny BEpiCs, mitigating RSV infection, and demonstrate that cytokine pretreatment can induce an adult-like immune-poised state in neonatal cells.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: This work suggests that interventions targeting basal stem cell programming or RIG-I induction could enhance RSV resistance, particularly in infants, and highlights the role of early-life infections in shaping lifelong epithelial antiviral defenses.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study relies on in vitro human cell models and mouse infection data, limiting direct translation to human infants, and does not address long-term durability or potential off-target effects of cytokine-induced immune-poised states, warranting cautious interpretation.

analysis.summary_en: This study addresses why RSV causes severe disease in infants but not adults by investigating age-related differences in bronchial epithelial cell responses. The authors demonstrate that adult bronchial basal stem cells and their progeny epithelial cells maintain robust RIG-I-STAT3 signaling that resists inactivation by RSV nonstructural protein 2, whereas infant cells are vulnerable due to lower RIG-I levels. Using mouse models, they show that acute respiratory viral infection triggers epigenetic and transcriptomic changes in epithelial cells that mimic adult-like states, and cytokine pretreatment can induce these protective states in neonatal cells. The findings reveal a lifelong imprinting mechanism where prior infections program basal stem cells to fortify antiviral defenses in progeny cells, offering potential avenues for therapeutic intervention to enhance RSV resistance in infants.

title_zh: 人支气管上皮细胞的免疫平衡状态介导成人对 RSV 的防御
source_body_en: Abstract Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) impairs STAT3 activation in infected ciliated cells in infants, but not adults, causing apoptosis to facilitate virus spread. How age regulates the STAT3 response to RSV in human bronchial epithelial cells (BEpiCs) is unknown. Here, we identify an age-associated immune-poised physiological state in human bronchial basal stem cells (BSCs) and progeny BEpiCs, rendering robust RIG-I to guard against the inactivation of RIG-I-STAT3 signaling by RSV nonstructural protein 2. In contrast, infant BEpiCs are vulnerable to such inactivation by RSV due to lower RIG-I levels. We show that acute respiratory viral infection in specific pathogen-free mice, rather than physical age, triggers sustained epigenetic and transcriptomic remodeling in BEpiCs that resembles age-associated changes in human BEpiCs. In addition, cytokine pretreatment of human neonatal BSCs induces an adult-like immune-poised state that is maintained in progeny BEpiCs to defend against RSV. Therefore, respiratory infection and inflammation during a lifetime imparts the effect of age to BSCs, which fortifies RIG-I in progeny cells to mitigate RSV infection. full_text: Abstract Introduction Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a major cause of lower respiratory tract infections, particularly among older adults. The recent introduction of adult RSV vaccines in Türkiye necessitates an assessment of physicians’ knowledge and recommendation behaviors regarding this new vaccine. This study aimed to evaluate physicians’ knowledge, attitudes, and early recommendation practices toward the RSV vaccine and to identify factors associated with vaccine recommendation. Materials and Methods This cross-sectional study was conducted via an online survey among 223 physicians across Türkiye using voluntary participation. Demographic characteristics, professional experience, and vaccination practices were analyzed using the Mann–Whitney U test and logistic regression analysis. Results The mean knowledge score was 7.6 ± 2.1 (on an 11-point scale), indicating moderate awareness. Only 10.3% of participants had recommended the RSV vaccine in the past 3 months, reflecting limited early uptake, while 42.6% were aware of its licensure for adults aged ≥60 years. Knowledge scores were significantly higher among faculty members and infectious diseases specialists compared with general practitioners and other specialties (p = 0.019 and p = 0.011, respectively). In multivariable analysis, higher knowledge score remained an independent predictor of vaccine recommendation (adjusted odds ratio = 1.54, 95% confidence interval: 1.12–2.11; p = 0.007). The most frequently reported barriers included lack of knowledge (76.2%), limited accessibility (44.4%), and reimbursement concerns (40.8%). Conclusion Despite generally positive attitudes toward RSV vaccination, early recommendation of the newly introduced adult RSV vaccine by physicians was limited. Clearer clinical guidance and educational support may be necessary to improve its adoption in clinical practice in Türkiye. Introduction Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a well-established cause of lower respiratory tract infections. Although historically associated with severe disease in infants, RSV also contributes substantially to morbidity, hospitalization, and mortality among adults aged ≥60 years and individuals with comorbidities[1-5]. Recent estimates indicate that RSV accounts for over 300,000 deaths annually in this age group worldwide[6, 7]. In Türkiye, national respiratory virus surveillance data show that RSV is consistently detected during seasonal viral circulation and may represent approximately 9%–10% of hospitalized cases of severe acute respiratory infection[8]. Hospital-based studies from Türkiye similarly suggest that RSV is a significant cause of respiratory morbidity among adults requiring hospitalization[9, 10]. These findings highlight that RSV constitutes a clinically relevant and potentially underrecognized burden in Türkiye, underscoring the need for effective preventive strategies, including adult vaccination[11]. RSV vaccines for adults have recently been licensed in multiple countries and became available for clinical use in Türkiye in May 2025. As healthcare professionals play a central role in vaccination programs, their awareness, knowledge, and willingness to recommend newly introduced vaccines are critical to real-world implementation[3, 12]. However, systematic data on physicians’ awareness of RSV vaccination in Türkiye remain limited. This study aimed to evaluate physicians’ knowledge, attitudes, and perceived barriers regarding RSV vaccination in Türkiye and to examine variations across specialties and levels of professional experience during the early implementation phase following vaccine introduction. Materials and Methods Study Design and Participants This cross-sectional study was conducted using an online survey between July 18 and August 10, 2025. Physicians involved in adult patient care across Türkiye were invited to participate. The target population included specialists in infectious diseases, internal medicine, pulmonology, family medicine, and related disciplines, as well as residents, general practitioners, and faculty members. The survey was developed using Google Forms and distributed through professional networks and social media platforms. A total of 223 physicians voluntarily completed the questionnaire. Sample Size Estimation Sample size estimation was performed prior to data collection using the standard formula for estimating a single population proportion in cross-sectional studies. As the true prevalence of adequate RSV knowledge and vaccine recommendation among physicians in Türkiye was unknown, a conservative prevalence estimate of 50% was used to ensure the maximum required sample size. Assuming a 95% confidence level and a 5% margin of error, the minimum required sample size was calculated to be 384 participants. To account for potential incomplete responses, the target sample size was increased to at least 400 physicians. However, a total of 223 physicians ultimately completed the survey, representing a broad range of specialties, professional levels, and healthcare settings. Although the final sample size was lower than the initial target, it is comparable to those reported in previous international physician surveys on adult vaccination and is considered adequate for descriptive reporting and exploratory analyses[13]. Questionnaire Development The questionnaire was developed based on a comprehensive review of the literature on RSV and adult vaccination practices[5, 12, 14-17]. The research team aimed to design a concise, practical instrument that could be completed within a limited time while capturing essential information on physicians’ knowledge, attitudes, and perceived barriers. The draft version was evaluated by infectious disease specialists, and minor revisions were implemented to enhance clarity and relevance. Each knowledge item was scored as 1 for a correct response and 0 for an incorrect response, yielding a maximum possible score of 11. The item assessing awareness of vaccine licensure was excluded from the knowledge score exclusively in the linear regression analysis, in which the knowledge score was treated as the dependent variable, to minimize the risk of collinearity. In contrast, in the logistic regression model, the total knowledge score (including this item) was retained as an independent variable. The final questionnaire comprised five main sections: (1) demographic and professional characteristics, (2) knowledge regarding RSV and its vaccination, (3) attitudes toward RSV vaccination, (4) perceived barriers to vaccine implementation, and (5) interest in further education on RSV and vaccination practices. The questionnaire was structured to ensure scientific rigor while maintaining practical feasibility, allowing busy physicians to complete it efficiently without compromising the reliability of the data obtained. The full questionnaire is provided in the Supplementary Materials. Several items, including those assessing vaccine recommendation practices, perceived barriers, clinical risk groups, and RSV-related complications, were designed as multiple-response questions, permitting participants to select more than one applicable option. Consequently, the percentages reported for these items may exceed 100%. Knowledge scores were analyzed as a continuous variable. The descriptive term “moderate,” as used in the Results section, reflects the mean score expressed as a percentage of the maximum possible score (approximately 69%), rather than a predefined categorical classification. Data Collection The survey was disseminated through professional networks. Participation was voluntary and anonymous, and no identifying information was collected. Accordingly, a nonprobability convenience sampling approach was employed. Electronic informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to survey completion. Ethics Approval This study was approved by the Ankara Bilkent City Hospital Medical Research Scientific and Ethical Review Board (TABED) (approval number: TABED 1-25-1519, approval date: 16.07.2025). Statistical Analysis Statistical analyses were conducted using IBM SPSS Statistics version 28.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Continuous variables were summarized as mean ± standard deviation or median with interquartile range, as appropriate, while categorical variables were presented as frequencies and percentages. Normality of data distribution was assessed visually and using the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. Comparisons of continuous variables between two groups were performed using the independent samples T-test or the Mann–Whitney U test, as appropriate. For comparisons involving more than two groups, one-way analysis of variance with Tukey’s HSD post hoc test was applied for normally distributed data, whereas the Kruskal–Wallis test with Dunn–Bonferroni post hoc correction was used for non-normally distributed data. Categorical variables were compared using the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test when expected cell counts were less than 5. Knowledge scores were compared across subgroups defined by professional status, specialty, and years of experience. A multivariable logistic regression model was constructed to identify independent predictors of RSV vaccine recommendation, including knowledge score, professional status, specialty, age, gender, and years of experience. The results were reported as odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). In addition, a multiple linear regression model was used to evaluate factors associated with higher knowledge scores. All statistical tests were two-sided, and a p-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results Participant Characteristics A total of 223 physicians routinely managing adult patients completed the survey. The mean age was 36.1 ± 8.8 years, and the majority were female (70.4%). Participants represented a range of professional positions, specialties, and workplace settings, with nearly half specializing in infectious diseases. Detailed demographic and professional characteristics are presented in Table 1. In terms of clinical practice, the median number of adult patients evaluated per week was 100 (interquartile range: 50–200), and most participants reported caring for patients aged ≥60 years. Knowledge Scores Overall, participants demonstrated a moderate level of knowledge, with a mean score of 7.6 ± 2.1. Knowledge scores differed significantly by professional status and specialty, with general practitioners scoring lower than specialists and faculty members (p = 0.019). No significant differences were observed according to years of professional experience (p = 0.114). Knowledge scores also varied across specialties (p = 0.011). Post hoc analyses revealed that infectious diseases physicians had significantly higher scores than physicians from other specialties (p = 0.046), whereas no other between-group differences were significant. A summary of knowledge scores across professional status, specialty, and experience subgroups is presented in Table 2. In an exploratory linear regression model, awareness of RSV vaccine licensure was independently associated with higher knowledge scores (β = 1.00, 95% CI: 0.50–1.50; p < 0.001), whereas professional position and years of experience were not significant predictors (Supplementary Table 1). Attitudes and Recent Practice Pneumococcal, influenza, and hepatitis B vaccines were the most frequently recommended vaccines for adults aged ≥60 years over the past 3 months. In this period, 29 participants (13.0%) reported not recommending any vaccine to adults in this age group. Here, “recommendation” refers to physician advice rather than confirmed prescription or administration. When asked about reasons for not recommending vaccines, 71.3% indicated that the item was not applicable, as they routinely recommend vaccines. Other reported barriers included not systematically reviewing patients’ vaccination records, lack of institutional protocols, and reimbursement or coverage issues. Detailed information on recommended vaccines and reasons for non-recommendation is provided in Supplementary Tables 2 and 3. Regarding RSV vaccination, 43.9% of participants stated that it should definitely be administered to adults aged ≥60 years; however, only a minority had recommended it in the past 3 months. Physicians who recommended the vaccine had significantly higher knowledge scores than those who did not (p = 0.004). Awareness of RSV vaccine licensure was limited, with fewer than half of participants correctly identifying approval for adults aged ≥60 years (Supplementary Table 4). As this item contributed to the overall knowledge score, physicians who answered correctly had higher total scores (p <0.001); therefore, licensure awareness was excluded as a separate variable in multivariable analyses to avoid collinearity. Awareness was slightly higher among infectious diseases specialists and faculty members, but overall familiarity with vaccine availability remained low, with only 31.4% knowing that the RSV vaccine was currently available in Türkiye. Subgroup distributions of physicians’ attitudes and practices regarding RSV vaccination are presented in Supplementary Table 4. Predictors of RSV Vaccine Recommendation In multivariable logistic regression (Table 3), higher knowledge scores were independently associated with RSV vaccine recommendation within the past 3 months (adjusted OR = 1.54, 95% CI: 1.12–2.11; p = 0.007). None of the other factors—including professional status, specialty, age, gender, or years of experience—were significantly associated. The model demonstrated good overall fit (Nagelkerke R2 = 0.19; Hosmer–Lemeshow p = 0.680). Barriers to RSV Vaccination Lack of knowledge was the most commonly reported barrier to recommending RSV vaccination across professional groups. Accessibility and reimbursement concerns were also frequently cited (Supplementary Table 5). Comparisons by professional status and specialty revealed significant differences in reported cost/reimbursement and accessibility concerns (p = 0.012 and p = 0.023, respectively) (Supplementary Tables 5 and 6). Most participants expressed interest in receiving further education or updates regarding RSV and its vaccines. Discussion This study evaluated physicians’ knowledge, attitudes, and recommendation practices regarding adult RSV vaccination in Türkiye during the early period following vaccine introduction. Conducted within the first three months of clinical availability, our findings provide an early snapshot of physician behavior toward RSV vaccination in adults aged ≥60 years. Although participants generally expressed favorable attitudes toward RSV vaccination and recognized RSV as a clinically important respiratory pathogen, actual recommendation rates remained limited. Overall, physicians demonstrated a moderate level of knowledge regarding RSV infection and its prevention. Despite this, only a minority actively recommended the vaccine to eligible patients. Similar gaps between awareness of disease severity and real-world vaccination practices have been reported in previous studies. A recent study from Türkiye highlighted ongoing knowledge gaps related to RSV prevention among healthcare professionals[18], while studies from Greece and the United States indicate that physicians may acknowledge the clinical importance of RSV yet remain hesitant to recommend vaccination during the early period following licensure[12, 13]. Early logistical and implementation challenges have also been documented across European healthcare systems[19]. Collectively, these findings suggest that awareness of disease severity alone may be insufficient to support early clinical adoption of newly introduced adult vaccines. In our multivariable analysis, higher knowledge scores were independently associated with a greater likelihood of RSV vaccine recommendation. Similarly, greater familiarity with RSV has been linked to higher recommendation rates in multivariable analyses conducted during the first season of RSV vaccine availability in other settings[12]. However, this relationship should be interpreted within the broader implementation context. The knowledge construct in this study encompassed not only general vaccine-related information but also awareness of local availability and clinical use. Accordingly, the frequently reported barrier of “lack of knowledge” may reflect uncertainty related to real-world implementation such as vaccine accessibility, procurement pathways, or institutional availability—rather than an absolute deficit in clinical knowledge about RSV. Within the Turkish healthcare system, structural factors including limited accessibility, absence of routine institutional delivery pathways, and lack of reimbursement may have contributed to the observed gap between awareness and recommendation behavior. At the time of the survey, RSV vaccines had recently been introduced for adult use but were not yet included in the national immunization program and were not reimbursed by the social security system. Similar practical challenges during early vaccine deployment have been reported in other healthcare systems[11, 19], and awareness of such factors may influence physicians’ likelihood of recommending vaccination in clinical practice. The observed gap between knowledge and recommendation behavior may therefore reflect early-stage adoption challenges rather than persistent reluctance among physicians. The absence of clearly defined national guidance regarding target populations and implementation pathways may have further contributed to hesitancy in active recommendations during this initial period. Nevertheless, this early assessment provides a valuable baseline for monitoring future changes as national communication strategies, reimbursement policies, and clinical guidance become more clearly established. full_text_sections.full_text: Abstract Introduction Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a major cause of lower respiratory tract infections, particularly among older adults. The recent introduction of adult RSV vaccines in Türkiye necessitates an assessment of physicians’ knowledge and recommendation behaviors regarding this new vaccine. This study aimed to evaluate physicians’ knowledge, attitudes, and early recommendation practices toward the RSV vaccine and to identify factors associated with vaccine recommendation. Materials and Methods This cross-sectional study was conducted via an online survey among 223 physicians across Türkiye using voluntary participation. Demographic characteristics, professional experience, and vaccination practices were analyzed using the Mann–Whitney U test and logistic regression analysis. Results The mean knowledge score was 7.6 ± 2.1 (on an 11-point scale), indicating moderate awareness. Only 10.3% of participants had recommended the RSV vaccine in the past 3 months, reflecting limited early uptake, while 42.6% were aware of its licensure for adults aged ≥60 years. Knowledge scores were significantly higher among faculty members and infectious diseases specialists compared with general practitioners and other specialties (p = 0.019 and p = 0.011, respectively). In multivariable analysis, higher knowledge score remained an independent predictor of vaccine recommendation (adjusted odds ratio = 1.54, 95% confidence interval: 1.12–2.11; p = 0.007). The most frequently reported barriers included lack of knowledge (76.2%), limited accessibility (44.4%), and reimbursement concerns (40.8%). Conclusion Despite generally positive attitudes toward RSV vaccination, early recommendation of the newly introduced adult RSV vaccine by physicians was limited. Clearer clinical guidance and educational support may be necessary to improve its adoption in clinical practice in Türkiye. Introduction Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a well-established cause of lower respiratory tract infections. Although historically associated with severe disease in infants, RSV also contributes substantially to morbidity, hospitalization, and mortality among adults aged ≥60 years and individuals with comorbidities[1-5]. Recent estimates indicate that RSV accounts for over 300,000 deaths annually in this age group worldwide[6, 7]. In Türkiye, national respiratory virus surveillance data show that RSV is consistently detected during seasonal viral circulation and may represent approximately 9%–10% of hospitalized cases of severe acute respiratory infection[8]. Hospital-based studies from Türkiye similarly suggest that RSV is a significant cause of respiratory morbidity among adults requiring hospitalization[9, 10]. These findings highlight that RSV constitutes a clinically relevant and potentially underrecognized burden in Türkiye, underscoring the need for effective preventive strategies, including adult vaccination[11]. RSV vaccines for adults have recently been licensed in multiple countries and became available for clinical use in Türkiye in May 2025. As healthcare professionals play a central role in vaccination programs, their awareness, knowledge, and willingness to recommend newly introduced vaccines are critical to real-world implementation[3, 12]. However, systematic data on physicians’ awareness of RSV vaccination in Türkiye remain limited. This study aimed to evaluate physicians’ knowledge, attitudes, and perceived barriers regarding RSV vaccination in Türkiye and to examine variations across specialties and levels of professional experience during the early implementation phase following vaccine introduction. Materials and Methods Study Design and Participants This cross-sectional study was conducted using an online survey between July 18 and August 10, 2025. Physicians involved in adult patient care across Türkiye were invited to participate. The target population included specialists in infectious diseases, internal medicine, pulmonology, family medicine, and related disciplines, as well as residents, general practitioners, and faculty members. The survey was developed using Google Forms and distributed through professional networks and social media platforms. A total of 223 physicians voluntarily completed the questionnaire. Sample Size Estimation Sample size estimation was performed prior to data collection using the standard formula for estimating a single population proportion in cross-sectional studies. As the true prevalence of adequate RSV knowledge and vaccine recommendation among physicians in Türkiye was unknown, a conservative prevalence estimate of 50% was used to ensure the maximum required sample size. Assuming a 95% confidence level and a 5% margin of error, the minimum required sample size was calculated to be 384 participants. To account for potential incomplete responses, the target sample size was increased to at least 400 physicians. However, a total of 223 physicians ultimately completed the survey, representing a broad range of specialties, professional levels, and healthcare settings. Although the final sample size was lower than the initial target, it is comparable to those reported in previous international physician surveys on adult vaccination and is considered adequate for descriptive reporting and exploratory analyses[13]. Questionnaire Development The questionnaire was developed based on a comprehensive review of the literature on RSV and adult vaccination practices[5, 12, 14-17]. The research team aimed to design a concise, practical instrument that could be completed within a limited time while capturing essential information on physicians’ knowledge, attitudes, and perceived barriers. The draft version was evaluated by infectious disease specialists, and minor revisions were implemented to enhance clarity and relevance. Each knowledge item was scored as 1 for a correct response and 0 for an incorrect response, yielding a maximum possible score of 11. The item assessing awareness of vaccine licensure was excluded from the knowledge score exclusively in the linear regression analysis, in which the knowledge score was treated as the dependent variable, to minimize the risk of collinearity. In contrast, in the logistic regression model, the total knowledge score (including this item) was retained as an independent variable. The final questionnaire comprised five main sections: (1) demographic and professional characteristics, (2) knowledge regarding RSV and its vaccination, (3) attitudes toward RSV vaccination, (4) perceived barriers to vaccine implementation, and (5) interest in further education on RSV and vaccination practices. The questionnaire was structured to ensure scientific rigor while maintaining practical feasibility, allowing busy physicians to complete it efficiently without compromising the reliability of the data obtained. The full questionnaire is provided in the Supplementary Materials. Several items, including those assessing vaccine recommendation practices, perceived barriers, clinical risk groups, and RSV-related complications, were designed as multiple-response questions, permitting participants to select more than one applicable option. Consequently, the percentages reported for these items may exceed 100%. Knowledge scores were analyzed as a continuous variable. The descriptive term “moderate,” as used in the Results section, reflects the mean score expressed as a percentage of the maximum possible score (approximately 69%), rather than a predefined categorical classification. Data Collection The survey was disseminated through professional networks. Participation was voluntary and anonymous, and no identifying information was collected. Accordingly, a nonprobability convenience sampling approach was employed. Electronic informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to survey completion. analysis.summary_en: This nationwide cross-sectional survey in Türkiye evaluated physicians' knowledge, attitudes, and early recommendation practices toward the newly introduced adult RSV vaccine. Among 223 physicians, the mean knowledge score was 7.6 out of 11, only 10.3% had recommended the vaccine in the prior three months, and 42.6% were aware of its licensure for adults aged 60 years or older. Knowledge scores were significantly higher among faculty members and infectious diseases specialists, and higher knowledge independently predicted vaccine recommendation (adjusted OR 1.54, 95% CI 1.12–2.11; p = 0.007). Barriers to recommendation included lack of knowledge (76.2%), limited accessibility (44.4%), and reimbursement concerns (40.8%). Despite generally positive attitudes, early uptake was limited, indicating a need for clearer clinical guidance and educational support to improve adoption in practice.
